entry.title: We can do better than line-buffered output
entry.summary: Buffered output typically comes in two flavors: fully buffered and line buffered. If output goes to a terminal then the implementation automatically selects line buffering, flushing its buffer when a line is completed so that it reaches the user immediately. Otherwise it fully buffers, holding output until the buffer is full or an explicit flush event at some arbitrary point in the future. Line buffering is a common bottleneck in non-interactive terminal applications such that it’s worth redirecting output to a file or pipe in order to avoid it. It doesn’t have to be this way. We can have our cake and eat it, too: promptly delivering lines to a terminal at fully-buffered speeds. For example, Info-ZIP unzip prints file names as it extract them from an archive. entry.title: Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age
entry.summary:
I’ve been fascinated with local LLMs for a couple of years now. The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular, higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued to popen(). This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own: Prospero. It’s written in my C++ style with a snappy Dear ImGui docking interface. entry.title: An LC-3 Disassembler in Haskell
entry.summary: LC-3 assembly is an educational programming language. It is simple enough that complex programs can be written directly in it without needing a compiler, and thus it is often used in teaching assembly. An LC-3 textual assembly program is compiled to a binary object file by an assembler, and then executed by a virtual machine. Writing a virtual machine for LC-3 is a fun little exercise. However, in this post, we implement a disassembler for compiled LC-3 binaries back to textual assembly programs.

entry.title: tugz: a new deflate library with three applications
entry.summary:
I spent a week creating a new deflate implementation from scratch in C named tugz to provide an Info-ZIP-compatible zip program for w64devkit 2.10.1 (released today). I also replaced busybox-w32’s deflate-based unzip, gzip, gunzip, and zcat apps as well. My new deflate performs much better than zlib and on par with libdeflate. In general the new programs are substantially faster and produce slightly smaller outputs than the BusyBox equivalents, which is optimized for size than speed after all, but also compared to the original gzip and Info-ZIP you get in a typical Linux distribution. The tugz programs are CRT-free (inspect them with peports!) with first-class Windows support and better Unicode handling.
Besides the cute logo, tugz is public domain and written entirely in my personal styl…
